title: Continuatio Fragmentorum ex Adversariis mathematicis depromptorum

deep.reconstruction:
PART 1 (end of item 105, from Adversaria I pp.113-115). Take a depressed cubic x^3 = f x + g whose three roots α, β, γ are all rational. Since the roots sum to 0, γ = -α-β. Let α and β be the roots of z^2 - p z + q = 0, so p = α+β, q = αβ, and p^2 - 4q = (α-β)^2 is a square. Multiplying this quadratic by z + p = z - γ gives z^3 + (q - p^2) z + p q = 0, so f = p^2 - q and g = -p q. The task is to restate the condition 'p^2 - 4q is a square' in terms of f and g. Euler multiplies p^2 - 4q by an undetermined square (p^2 + α q)^2; here α and β are reused as new unknown coefficients. He then matches the product with f^3 + β g^2 = p^6 - 3p^4 q + (3+β) p^2 q^2 - q^3. Comparing coefficients: 2α - 4 = -3 gives α = 1/2. Then α^2 - 8α = -15/4 = 3 + β gives β = -27/4. The last coefficient checks: -4α^2 = -1. The identity is f^3 - (27/4) g^2 = (p^2 - 4q)(p^2 + q/2)^2. In modern terms this is the discriminant: 4f^3 - 27g^2 = (α-β)^2 (β-γ)^2 (γ-α)^2. So 'three rational roots' implies 'f^3 - 27g^2/4 is a rational square'. Euler adds two remarks. (1) The square must be an integer square: integer roots force g = -αβ(α+β) to be even. (2) An equation of the form v^3 = 4f v + 8g must first be reduced by v = 2x to x^3 = f x + g. Remark (2) is precisely what excludes the scaled casus-irreducibilis example x^3 = 12x - 8 (that is, 2·2cos(2π/9) and its conjugates), whose value 1296 = 36^2 would otherwise pass.

PART 2 (item 106, Krafft; Adversaria I pp.162-164). Let s = Σ_{n≥0} (-1)^n/(1+na) = ∫_0^1 dt/(1+t^a). Euler squares the series by grouping the Cauchy-product terms along diagonals |n-m| = k:
s^2 = Σ 1/(1+na)^2 + 2 Σ_{k≥1} (-1)^k T_k, where T_k = Σ_n 1/((1+na)(1+(n+k)a)).
Partial fractions and telescoping give T_k = (1/(ka)) Σ_{j=0}^{k-1} 1/(1+ja). This yields A = 1/a and B = (1/2a)(1 + 1/(1+a)), with C and the rest on the next page. The remaining alternating 'harmonic' sum is summed on the next page by a generating function z(x), a substitution x = y^a, two differentiations and integration. The result is
s^2 = Σ 1/(1+na)^2 - 2 ∫_0^1 [y^{a-2}/(1+y^a)] ∫_0^y dt/(1+t^a) dy.
- For a = 2 this gives Σ 1/(2n+1)^2 = π^2/8.
- For a = 1 it gives (log 2)^2 = π^2/6 - 2∫_0^1 log(1+y)/(y(1+y)) dy.
The a = 1 identity checks numerically: the integral equals π^2/12 - (log 2)^2/2.
errors: Not an error on this page itself, where the condition is stated only as 'requiritur', i.e. necessary. But it bears on the preceding page (Obs. III), which claims the criterion is also sufficient. A square discriminant with integer f and even g is necessary but NOT sufficient for rational roots: cyclic (Galois group A3) cubics also have square discriminant. Euler's normalization (2°) removes the 2-scaled cases such as x^3 = 12x - 8. It does not remove fields in which 2 splits. Counterexample: x^3 = 93x + 124, the depressed form (X = 3x+1) of the conductor-31 cyclic cubic x^3 + x^2 - 10x - 8. Here f = 93 is not divisible by 4 and g is even, and f^3 - (27/4)g^2 = 804357 - 103788 = 700569 = 837^2, an integer square. Yet the cubic is irreducible: none of ±1, ±2, ±4, ±8 is a root. On the previous page's scale (x^3 = 3·31x + 2·62, with 31 = 2^2 + 3·3^2), this is exactly the 'other' representation g = α^3 + 3αβ^2 = fα, which Euler listed and then silently discarded in Obs. II. His claim there that g must equal ±(α^3 - 9αβ^2) overlooks that g + ν√-3 need not be a cube in Z[ω].
Notation clash: α and β denote the roots and then are reused as the undetermined coefficients in the matching. This is harmless but confusing.
In the display for A the first term is printed 1/(1+a); by the pattern it should be 1/(1·(1+a)). The value A = 1/a is correct with that reading.

Item 106: the regrouping of the conditionally convergent double series along diagonals is not justified. The resulting diagonal series (terms ~ (log k)/k, alternating) does converge, and the a = 1 and a = 2 results check out.

ideas.what: Expressing the square-root condition for rational roots of x^3 = fx + g as f^3 - 27g^2/4 = □, via the identity f^3 - (27/4)g^2 = (p^2 - 4q)(p^2 + q/2)^2 found by undetermined coefficients
ideas.modern_name: Discriminant of a cubic is the square of the Vandermonde product; square discriminant is a necessary condition for all roots rational
ideas.usually_credited_to: Cubic discriminant in Cardano's formula (16th c.); square-discriminant/Galois-group link: Lagrange, Galois
ideas.where_published: Euler, Opera postuma I (1862), E819; related to Euler's algebra of cubics (Vollständige Anleitung zur Algebra) - unsure whether this criterion appears there

ideas.what: Integrality/parity refinement (g even) and reduction v = 2x as extra conditions
ideas.modern_name: Elementary 2-adic normalization of the depressed cubic
ideas.where_published: E819 only, as far as known

ideas.what: Squaring an alternating series Σ(-1)^n/(1+na) by diagonal grouping of the Cauchy product, with telescoping of the diagonals
ideas.modern_name: Cauchy product / Euler sums Σ(-1)^k H_k(a)/k
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (alternating Euler sums); the 'square the Leibniz series to get Σ1/(2n+1)^2' proof is often presented as a modern classroom proof

ideas.what: General identity (∫_0^1 dt/(1+t^a))^2 = Σ 1/(1+na)^2 - 2∫_0^1 y^{a-2}/(1+y^a) ∫_0^y dt/(1+t^a) dy, specialized to a = 2 (π^2/8) and a = 1
ideas.modern_name: Integral representation of an alternating Euler sum / ψ'-type series

missed.claim: Euler's discriminant criterion, together with the integrality refinement and the v = 2x reduction he adds on this page, is still not sufficient for rational roots. The explicit counterexample x^3 = 93x + 124 (conductor-31 cyclic cubic) comes exactly from the alternative cube representation he discarded on the previous page. The refinements show Euler was aware of scaled casus-irreducibilis cases but missed fields in which 2 splits.
missed.quote: De hoc autem criterio duo sunt notanda: 1° f^3 - 27/4 gg debet esse quadratum integrum; 2° hujusmodi aequationes v^3 = 4fv + 8g ... debent reduci
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: This is a historical correction: the sufficiency claim in E819 (Obs. III) is false, with a concrete counterexample. It is an early, unrecognized brush with cyclic cubic fields. It is of minor mathematical novelty.

missed.claim: A general-parameter squaring of Σ(-1)^n/(1+na) yields a one-parameter family of identities. These include a Cauchy-product proof of Σ1/(2n+1)^2 = π^2/8 and an evaluation tying (log 2)^2 to ζ(2). The squared-Leibniz-series proof is often attributed to modern authors.
missed.quote: Si habeatur haec series s = 1/1 - 1/(1+a) + 1/(1+2a) - ... ejus quadratum s^2 commode per seriem exprimere
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: This may be an Euler/Krafft precedent for a 'modern' elementary proof of the Basel-type sum. Whether it is noted in Opera Omnia commentary is unsure.

deep.surprise_reason: The cubic part is routine discriminant algebra. Its interest is that Euler's added refinements still fail, via a clean conductor-31 counterexample the literature may not attach to E819. The Krafft squaring method is a nice, possibly under-cited precedent for a known elementary proof of π^2/8, but nothing here would astonish a specialist.
transcription_corrections: The transcription matches the image well. In A's display the first term is printed 1/(1+a); it is presumably intended as 1/(1·(1+a)), an error in the original, not the OCR.
'p^4 + 2αppq + ααqq' is (pp + αq)^2, consistent with the image.
